classification.difficultyReason: Choose favourable card combinations, then use independent replacement draws with order multiplicities and disjoint diamond cases.

content.prompt: From a standard pack of 52 cards, three are selected at random. Find the probability that:

children.label: a
children.prompt: they are the jack of spades, the two of clubs and the seven of diamonds,

answer.worked:
There is one favourable three-card selection.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\frac{1}{\binom{52}{3}}\\&=\frac{1}{22100}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: all three are aces,

answer.worked:
Choose three of the four aces.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\frac{\binom{4}{3}}{\binom{52}{3}}\\&=\frac{4}{22100}\\&=\frac{1}{5525}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: they are all diamonds,

answer.worked:
Choose three of the thirteen diamonds.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\frac{\binom{13}{3}}{\binom{52}{3}}\\&=\frac{286}{22100}\\&=\frac{11}{850}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: they are all of the same suit,

answer.worked:
Choose one of four suits, then three cards of that suit.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\frac{4\binom{13}{3}}{\binom{52}{3}}\\&=\frac{1144}{22100}\\&=\frac{22}{425}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: they are all picture cards,

answer.worked:
There are twelve picture cards: four jacks, four queens and four kings.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\frac{\binom{12}{3}}{\binom{52}{3}}\\&=\frac{220}{22100}\\&=\frac{11}{1105}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: two are red and one is black,

answer.worked:
Choose two of the twenty-six red cards and one of the twenty-six black cards.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\frac{\binom{26}{2}\binom{26}{1}}{\binom{52}{3}}\\&=\frac{8450}{22100}\\&=\frac{13}{34}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: g
children.prompt: one is a seven, one is an eight and one is a nine,

answer.worked:
Choose one card from each of the three ranks; each rank has four cards.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\frac{\binom{4}{1}\binom{4}{1}\binom{4}{1}}{\binom{52}{3}}\\&=\frac{64}{22100}\\&=\frac{16}{5525}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: h
children.prompt: two are sevens and one is a six,

answer.worked:
Choose two of the four sevens and one of the four sixes.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\frac{\binom{4}{2}\binom{4}{1}}{\binom{52}{3}}\\&=\frac{24}{22100}\\&=\frac{6}{5525}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: i
children.prompt: exactly one is a diamond,

answer.worked:
Choose one diamond and two of the thirty-nine non-diamonds.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\frac{\binom{13}{1}\binom{39}{2}}{\binom{52}{3}}\\&=\frac{9633}{22100}\\&=\frac{741}{1700}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: j
children.prompt: at least two of them are diamonds.

answer.worked:
The disjoint cases are two diamonds and one non-diamond, or three diamonds.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\frac{\binom{13}{2}\binom{39}{1}+\binom{13}{3}}{\binom{52}{3}}\\&=\frac{3042+286}{22100}\\&=\frac{64}{425}.\end{aligned}$$

children.prompt: Now the three cards are selected from the same pack one at a time, and each card is replaced before the next one is drawn. Find the probability that:

children.label: k
children.prompt: they are the jack of spades, the two of clubs and the seven of diamonds,

answer.worked:
The three specified cards can occur in $3!$ different orders. Each order has probability $(\frac{1}{52})^3$, since each card is replaced before the next draw.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=3!\left(\frac{1}{52}\right)^3\\&=\frac{3}{70304}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: l
children.prompt: all three are aces,

answer.worked:
Replacement makes the draws independent, with four aces available on every draw.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\left(\frac{4}{52}\right)^3\\&=\frac{1}{2197}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: m
children.prompt: they are all diamonds,

answer.worked:
Each independent draw has probability $\frac{13}{52}$ of being a diamond.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\left(\frac{13}{52}\right)^3\\&=\frac{1}{64}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: n
children.prompt: they are all of the same suit,

answer.worked:
All three cards can belong to any one of four suits; these cases are disjoint.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=4\left(\frac{13}{52}\right)^3\\&=\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: o
children.prompt: they are all picture cards,

answer.worked:
There are twelve picture cards available on every independent draw.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\left(\frac{12}{52}\right)^3\\&=\frac{27}{2197}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: p
children.prompt: two are red and one is black,

answer.worked:
The black card can occur in any of three draw positions.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=3\left(\frac{26}{52}\right)^2\left(\frac{26}{52}\right)\\&=\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: q
children.prompt: one is a seven, one is an eight and one is a nine,

answer.worked:
The three distinct ranks can occur in $3!$ orders. Each required rank has probability $\frac{4}{52}$ on its draw.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=3!\left(\frac{4}{52}\right)^3\\&=\frac{6}{2197}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: r
children.prompt: two are sevens and one is a six,

answer.worked:
The six can occur in any of three draw positions. Each required rank has probability $\frac{4}{52}$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=3\left(\frac{4}{52}\right)^2\left(\frac{4}{52}\right)\\&=\frac{3}{2197}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: s
children.prompt: exactly one is a diamond,

answer.worked:
The diamond can occur in any of three draw positions; the other two draws must be non-diamonds.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=3\left(\frac{13}{52}\right)\left(\frac{39}{52}\right)^2\\&=\frac{27}{64}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: t
children.prompt: at least two of them are diamonds.

answer.worked:
Add the disjoint cases of exactly two diamonds and three diamonds. For exactly two, the non-diamond has three possible positions.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=3\left(\frac{13}{52}\right)^2\left(\frac{39}{52}\right)+\left(\frac{13}{52}\right)^3\\&=\frac{9}{64}+\frac{1}{64}\\&=\frac{5}{32}.\end{aligned}$$
